content_html:
Why We Photograph

External Record × Internal Expression × Relational/Empty Process

We photograph to explain and to express — but every photograph ultimately works in the relational middle: an index of the outside world shaped by inner intention, made meaningful through context and interpretation.

External Record Internal Expression Relational / Empty Process
Claim:
Photos indexically capture the world; they explain external reality.		 Photos encode intention, mood, memory; they express inner reality. Meaning is neither in the object nor the subject alone; it arises dependently.
Use cases:
journalism, science imaging, evidence, documentation.		 art, diary, therapy, identity work. curatorial practice, participatory media, cross‑cultural projects.
Strength:
indexical link (light from scene → sensor/film).		 reveals perspective; invites empathy and affect. integrates context (caption, display, viewer history).
Risk:
naive realism (“the camera never lies”).		 solipsism or over‑projection. relativism if context is ignored / unstated.
Memory link:
cue for reconstructing events.		 cue for reconstructing feelings and self‑narrative. both event and feeling co‑arise in recall; meaning is emergent.
Theory hooks:
evidential index; documentary realism.		 Barthes’ punctum; expressionism. Dependent origination; semiotics; enactive cognition.

Meaning is co‑constructed: the same image can function as evidence, expression, and relation depending on viewing conditions.

References

  • Barthes, R. (1981). Camera Lucida: Reflections on Photography. Hill and Wang.
  • Gethin, R. (1998). The Foundations of Buddhism. Oxford University Press.
  • Schacter, D. L. (1999). The seven sins of memory: Insights from psychology and cognitive neuroscience. American Psychologist, 54(3), 182–203. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.54.3.182
  • Sontag, S. (1977). On Photography. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
  • Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience. MIT Press.
